The passage describes the Treaty of Tordesillas, which divided newly discovered lands between Spain and Portugal along a meridian west of the Cape Verde Islands. Spain received territories west of the line, which included the Americas as later understood, while Portugal received territories to the east, including parts of Africa and the route to India.  

The Spanish monarchs would have insisted on control west of the line because they knew of Columbus’s 1492 voyage, which they believed reached Asia (the “Indies”), but they were also aware Portugal had already established trade routes and claims along the African coast and toward India. Securing the western route ensured they could claim lands encountered there without Portuguese interference.  

Option (D) fits best: the Spanish likely believed that claiming the western route (and the lands there) was strategically more feasible than challenging Portugal’s established eastern trade network and presence near India.  

Final answer: (D)
